extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and anyone tasked with forming or evaluating technical definitions/terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming precise, useful definitions of terms in philosophy and science, including when to adhere to received usage, when to restrict or reform meanings, and how to select distinguishing properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition should agree with received use
rubrics_metrics.description: The fixed and precise connotation which [a term] receives should not be in deviation from, but in agreement (as far as it goes) with, the vague and fluctuating connotation which the term already had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, define a name in accordance with its received use; aim to fix connotation without rendering received assertions inadmissible. Only redefine radically when justified by deeper knowledge. (Avoid arbitrarily choosing meanings that break established propositions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Define by ascertaining common attributes via comparison/induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To fix the connotation of a concrete name ... is to define the name. This ... supposes a comparison of the things, feature by feature and property by property, to ascertain what attributes they agree in; and not unfrequently an operation strictly inductive, for the purpose of ascertaining some unobvious agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select properties after systematic comparison of class members; use induction to reveal non-obvious commonalities that justify grouping and naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select properties that serve as sure marks or causes of others
rubrics_metrics.description: We should therefore select from among the common properties ... those on which it has been ascertained by experience, or proved by deduction, that many others depend; or at least which are sure marks of them, and from whence, therefore, many others will follow by inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitional marks that are either causal or reliable indicators of many other properties rather than merely those most familiar. Example: choose a property that explains or predicts other attributes of the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer well-known predicates but balance with discriminatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: Our choice is first limited by the preference to be given to properties which are well known, and familiarly predicated of the class; but even these are often too numerous to be all included in the definition, and, besides, the properties most generally known may not be those which serve best to mark out the class from all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, use familiar predicates in definitions for accessibility, but ensure they effectively distinguish the class; do not rely solely on familiarity if they fail to mark the kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must serve some proposition or principle (avoid arbitrary isolated definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases there is a tacit assumption of some proposition which is to be expressed by means of the definition... A definition of [a term] which was not employed to express some principle, would be of no value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good definition is judged by the role it plays in validating or expressing important propositions; ask what principle the definition is meant to enunciate. Avoid defining terms in isolation of their theoretical or practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve truth of propositions in which the term is used
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition is propounded to us as a useful step in knowledge, we are always entitled to ask what principle it serves to enunciate... the question really is, how the conception shall be understood and defined in order that the proposition may be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the chosen connotation keeps true (or intended) propositions involving the term. Example: definition of 'uniform force' was chosen so gravity would continue to be an instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as part of discovery—defer finality until theory matures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to frame a perfect set of definitions on any subject, until the theory of the subject is perfect; and as science makes progress, its definitions are also progressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that definitions may need revision as knowledge advances; avoid treating early definitions as immutable; consider definition as a stage in theory-building rather than the final word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to define by non-obvious properties when they best mark the class
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often necessary to define the class by some property not familiarly known, provided that property be the best mark of those which are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject less-obvious but explanatorily powerful properties as definitional marks (example: De Blainville's definition of life by continuous decomposition and recomposition). Balance accessibility with theoretical adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When fixing a vague term, prefer restriction over extension
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better, in such a case, to give a fixed connotation to the term by restricting, than by extending its use; rather excluding from the epithet Beautiful some things to which it is commonly considered applicable, than leaving out of its connotation any of the qualities by which ... the general mind may have been habitually guided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve significant aspects of a term's meaning, narrow denotation rather than broaden it when choosing a fixed connotation. Avoid definitions that convert a rich term into an overly broad, trivial category (e.g., defining 'beautiful' merely as 'agreeable').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard historical connotations without deep knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: In attempting to rectify the use of a vague term by giving it a fixed connotation, we must take care not to discard (unless advisedly, and on the ground of a deeper knowledge of the subject) any portion of the connotation which the word ... previously carried with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect language as the conservator of ancient experience; study past usages and associated propositions before redefining. If a proposed definition would render once-accepted true propositions false, require thorough historical and evidential justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep meanings alive by predication and preserving associated predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Words naturally retain much more of their meaning to persons of active imagination... To minds of a different description, the only antidote to this corruption of language is predication. The habit of predicating of the name, all the various properties which it originally connoted, keeps up the association between the name and those properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain complex meanings by using the term with explicit predicates that remind users of its fuller connotation; ensure the predicates themselves retain their associations. Avoid rote repetition of formulas that no longer carry vivid meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate word-history because dictionaries are blunt guides
rubrics_metrics.description: The dictionary meaning is marked out in a broad, blunt way ... The history of a word, by showing the causes which determine its use, is in these cases a better guide to its employment than any definition; for definitions can only show its meaning at the particular time, or at most the series of its successive meanings, but its history may show the law by which the succession was produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before fixing or criticizing a definition, examine the historical sequence of usages and the causal reasons for changes. Use etymology and historical context to judge whether associations are essential or accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and analyze transitive/derivative applications of words
rubrics_metrics.description: The applications which a word acquires by this gradual extension of it from one set of objects to another ... Stewart calls its transitive applications... Where the association is so natural and habitual as to become virtually indissoluble, the transitive meanings will coalesce in one complex conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to senses that have arisen by gradual transference; determine whether different applications share a real common property or are merely linked by associative chains. Avoid forcing a single genus on genuinely ambiguous senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of losing meaning through habitual, partial activation
rubrics_metrics.description: A word originally associated with a very complex cluster of ideas, is far from calling up all those ideas in the mind, every time the word is used; it calls up only one or two ... so that words so used come in time to be no longer capable of suggesting any other of the ideas appropriated to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cognitive habits that narrow a word's effective connotation over time. Take corrective measures (education, predication, contested usage) to revive dormant aspects of meaning when they are valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider practical consequences of redefining: do not let useful old formulas vanish
rubrics_metrics.description: While the formulas remain, the meaning may at any time revive; ... When the words in their original acceptation connoted ... a complication of outward facts and inward feelings, ... it is natural and inevitable that in every age a certain portion of our recorded and traditional knowledge ... should fall asleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before redefining, consider whether losing an older nuance would erase useful guidance embedded in traditional formulas or maxims. Use caution: discarding such connotations can impede future recovery of important insights.
